entry.title: UC San Diego Engineers Develop Light-Based Magnetism Control for Faster Memory
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Engineers at the University of California San Diego have demonstrated a method for controlling magnetism using shaped laser light, overcoming previous thickness and polarization barriers in optical switching. By shrinking and reshaping ultrafast laser beams, the researchers successfully induced deterministic magnetic switching in a nine-layer cobalt and platinum structure without needing specific light polarization.

While traditional magnetic memory relies on external fields that limit writing speed and consume high energy, optical switching could theoretically achieve speeds over 1,000 times greater. However, significant engineering challenges remain before the specialized ultrafast lasers used in the experiments can be integrated into practical computer hardware.

entry.title: Jordan Valley Archaeological Site 'Ubeidiya Dated to at Least 1.9 Million Years Ago
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers have redated the archaeological site of 'Ubeidiya in the Jordan Valley to at least 1.9 million years ago, pushing back the timeline of early human migration into the Levant by hundreds of thousands of years. Using a combination of cosmogenic isotope burial dating, paleomagnetism, and uranium-lead dating of fossilized freshwater snail shells, the team established that the site is contemporaneous with early human activity at Dmanisi in Georgia.

The updated timeline indicates that early human populations expanded out of Africa during a crucial early period, bringing distinct stone tool traditions—including both Oldowan and Acheulean technologies—into new regions. Accounting for a complex history of Pleistocene sediment recycling within the Dead Sea rift resolved initial discrepancies in isotope measurements, strengthening the reliability of the new chronological framework.

entry.title: University of Bonn Researchers Discover Two Distinct Sleep Stages in Australian Jumping Spiders
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at the University of Bonn have found that the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata experiences distinct sleep stages, including a phase closely resembling rapid eye movement (REM) sleep in vertebrates. Using infrared cameras and behavioral response tests under various lighting conditions, the team observed that the spiders exhibit muscle twitches and characteristic eye movements during sleep, while also demonstrating sleep rebound after periods of sleep disruption.

The findings provide experimental confirmation that these spiders engage in genuine, regulated sleep rather than simple resting behavior. While the presence of REM-like movements does not confirm that spiders dream, the discovery offers new insight into the evolution and complexity of sleep across different nervous systems, opening avenues for future research into how sleep supports cognitive functions and is affected by environmental factors.

entry.title: Google DeepMind AI Model Outperforms Traditional Weather Models in Hurricane Isaias Forecasts
entry.content:
Links: npr.org | source

Meteorologists and hurricane experts report that artificial intelligence models, specifically Google DeepMind's system, are rapidly transforming weather forecasting. When Hurricane Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 storm in early October, the Google DeepMind AI model accurately predicted its path toward the western Florida Panhandle while conventional physics-based models incorrectly projected a more westward track toward southeastern Louisiana.

While traditional models rely on real-time atmospheric data and complex physical equations, AI models analyze thousands of historical storms using neural networks to identify patterns. The National Hurricane Center incorporated Google's model into its operational forecasts beginning last year, though forecasters continue to use a blend of models and human expertise because the AI system was less effective at predicting storm intensity compared to its accuracy in tracking paths.

entry.title: Study of 709 BCE Total Solar Eclipse Refines Earth Rotation and Solar Activity Models
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

An international research team has analyzed records of a total solar eclipse from 709 BCE preserved in ancient Chinese historical texts to reconstruct Earth's historical rotation speed. By correcting an eight-kilometer error in the geographic coordinates of the ancient Lu capital of Qufu, the scientists calculated a delta T value between 20,264 and 21,204 seconds, providing more precise constraints on how fast Earth spun during the eighth through sixth centuries BCE.

Investigators also examined a later historical addendum from the Book of Han describing the eclipsed Sun as "completely yellow above and below," interpreting it as a possible early written account of the solar corona. This observation aligns with radiocarbon-based tree ring reconstructions suggesting the Sun was transitioning out of a prolonged period of low activity known as the Neo Assyrian Grand Minimum.

entry.title: Dianjunus Rex Giant Fungus Discovered in China
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Scientists have discovered a new giant fungal species, Dianjunus rex (nicknamed "D-rex"), in the forests of Yunnan, China. Producing upright reproductive structures reaching up to 50 centimeters in height and weighing up to 2.2 kilograms, it represents the largest known fruiting bodies within the phylum Ascomycota and establishes an entirely new genus and family, Dianjunaceae.

Genetic analysis and molecular clock estimates indicate that the lineage of Dianjunus rex originated approximately 65 million years ago, roughly one million years after the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. Researchers suggest that the dramatic ecological disruption and sudden abundance of dead plant material following the extinction event created unique opportunities for wood-decomposing fungi, potentially driving the evolution of its large spore-dispersal structures.

entry.title: University of Illinois Researchers Develop First 3D Thermal Invisibility Cloak
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers have developed and tested the first three-dimensional thermal invisibility cloak capable of concealing objects from infrared cameras and extreme temperatures from any direction. Constructed from a hybrid aluminum-and-rubber lattice material, the device directs heat around a hidden object rather than simply blocking it, creating a uniform thermal profile that makes the object appear absent to infrared imaging.

Published in Nature Communications, the breakthrough overcomes the geometric and directional limitations of earlier two-dimensional thermal cloaks. The technology could improve thermal management in microchips, protect sensitive electronics from harsh environments, and offer new methods for thermal stealth, with future research aiming to adapt the design for objects that generate their own heat.

entry.title: Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Filmed Melting in Real Time to Advance Brain-Like Computing
entry.content:

Researchers have recorded the real-time melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice while simultaneously manipulating the shape and size of individual skyrmions. Conducted primarily at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz alongside contributions from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, the study offers unprecedented insight into the dynamics of these microscopic magnetic vortices.

Skyrmions are nanoscale magnetic structures that could enable high-density data storage, quantum technologies, and brain-like neuromorphic computing architectures operating with drastically reduced electricity consumption. By demonstrating precise, real-time control over how these ordered lattices break apart and behave individually, the findings help overcome fundamental obstacles toward developing practical spintronic computing devices.

entry.title: Max Planck Institute Researchers Discover Three Supermassive Black Holes in Distant Galaxy
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered three actively feeding supermassive black holes in the distant galaxy J0148-4214, located more than 12.5 billion light-years from Earth. Led by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, an international team identified the system by analyzing high-speed hydrogen gas movements using integral field spectroscopy.

Two of the black holes reside near the galaxy's center and are projected to merge within the next few hundred million years, while a third sits further out and may have been displaced by an earlier gravitational recoil. The discovery provides rare evidence of how efficient early universe processes were at bringing massive black holes together, helping explain their rapid growth shortly after the Big Bang.

entry.title: Yale University Study Suggests Spinosaurus Spent Most of Life Underwater
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at Yale University have developed a machine learning approach to reconstruct the lifestyles of extinct vertebrates, concluding that the predatory dinosaur Spinosaurus spent the vast majority of its life submerged underwater. By analyzing skeletal measurements from hundreds of fossil and modern specimens alongside a statistical method originally developed during World War II, the team evaluated limb proportions to predict soft-tissue swimming adaptations and aquatic habits with high accuracy.

The findings provide new support for a heavily aquatic interpretation of Spinosaurus, contrasting with other ancient marine reptiles like mesosaurs, whose limb proportions indicate they regularly moved between land and water. The researchers found that all Paleozoic marine reptiles retained amphibious habits and regularly returned to land, highlighting distinct evolutionary pathways in secondary aquatic adaptation.

Chemical and genetic testing revealed that the mushroom lacks known psychoactive compounds like psilocybin, pointing to an entirely unfamiliar hallucinogenic substance.

Genomic analysis of 53 specimens across the broader Lanmaoa genus also uncovered four previously unknown species, demonstrating how field research and museum collections can reveal new biological diversity. Isolating the mushroom's mysterious active compound could provide researchers with a novel tool to investigate the neurological mechanisms that generate complex visual hallucinations in humans.

entry.title: University of Warwick Researchers Challenge 40-Year Superconductor Assumption
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at the University of Warwick have discovered that copper-based cuprate superconductors, long assumed to possess a uniform crystal structure, actually contain a complex patchwork of different atomic arrangements. Using scanning three-dimensional X-ray diffraction at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, the team mapped interior structural variations and found boundary regions hundreds of times wider than previously expected.

Published in Physical Review Letters, the findings challenge four decades of scientific assumptions built on the premise of uniform interior structures. The unexpected internal complexity and unusually broad transition zones may actively interfere with electrical performance, indicating that prior bulk measurements and theoretical models will need to be reevaluated.

Statistical comparisons of its limb proportions indicate that the species was ground-dwelling and likely incapable of flight, representing the earliest known example of a bird lineage losing its flying ability. The findings challenge the assumption that early avian evolution was strictly directed toward improved flight, demonstrating that prehistoric birds rapidly diversified into various ecological niches and terrestrial lifestyles.

Researchers analyzing multi-angle video recordings found that these small reptiles reach peak forward velocities between 1.72 and 3.69 meters per second while executing the maneuver.

To achieve high-speed rolling without a mechanical wheel axle, the snakes coordinate complex body movements by alternating side-to-side strokes while keeping their heads remarkably stable and pointed forward. This specialized separation of function demonstrates how precise muscular control and behavioral innovation can enable forms of locomotion that seem physically improbable given an animal's anatomy.

entry.title: University of Strathclyde and Durham University Researchers Propose Mirror Life Detection Method
entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers from the University of Strathclyde and Durham University have proposed a detection method for "mirror life," a hypothetical form of life built from reversed molecular structures. The technique utilizes circularly polarized luminescence (CPL)—the same foundational concept used in 3D movie glasses—to analyze light emitted with specific left- and right-handed properties by specialized fluorescent probes attached inside cells.

Although mirror life does not currently exist, experts view its potential creation as a serious biosecurity concern because synthetic reversed organisms could interact unpredictably with Earth's ecosystems and evade natural defenses. The proposed CPL assay offers a contingency screening approach using ordinary biological samples, allowing scientists to develop detection capabilities and support potential future biosecurity regulations before any such organisms emerge.

Implemented within the open-source WEST simulation program, the approach resolved a long-standing discrepancy in silicon carbide by showing that internal conversion has a larger impact on excited triplet state lifetimes than previously estimated. This predictive capability could assist in designing better quantum qubits and materials for renewable energy storage, with ongoing efforts exploring machine learning to further enhance simulation efficiency.

entry.content:
Links: sciencedaily.com | source

Researchers at ETH Zurich analyzing samples collected from asteroid Bennu by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission have found that the asteroid formed near the water-ice line in the early Solar System about 4.5 billion years ago. Isotope analysis of iron, titanium, and chromium revealed that Bennu shares a close chemical relationship with asteroid Ryugu and rare CI meteorites, pointing to a hybrid origin from both inner and outer Solar System materials.

The findings challenge earlier assumptions that primitive asteroids originated exclusively in the outer Solar System. The researchers propose that Jupiter's rapid early growth acted as a structural barrier, limiting the movement of larger particles while allowing fine dust to mix near the water-ice boundary, preserving chemical signatures closely resembling the elemental composition of the Sun.

entry.title: Kadoa Report Finds Investor-Owned Utilities Charge 23% More For Electricity Than Public Providers
entry.content:
Links: kadoa.com | hacker news

In 2025, residential electricity customers paid an average of 17.8 cents per kilowatt-hour at investor-owned utilities, compared to 14.5 cents at public utilities and 14.1 cents at co-ops. Since 2020, investor-owned utility prices increased by 34%, outpacing both public utility price growth of 19% and general inflation of 24%.

The widening price gap primarily developed between 2020 and 2023 during a broad energy price spike, with investor-owned rates rising 25% while nonprofit utility rates rose 11%. Investor-owned utilities build shareholder returns into their rate structures, whereas public utilities and co-ops operate without shareholders and often benefit from tax exemptions and tax-free borrowing.
